items.title: Focus Question: What forces affect a soccer ball's trajectory after it is kicked?

answer.html: Once the ball leaves the foot, only gravity (a downward force, 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>= 𝑚𝑔) acts if air resistance is ignored. Air drag (a force from the air that opposes the motion) also acts in real life but is small enough to ignore here. The foot's force acts only during the kick.

items.title: Get It? (Illustrate): sketches of a water balloon launched by a slingshot from behind, above, and the side

question.html: Behind the launcher (looking along the line of the shot): the balloon goes straight up and then straight down, like a ball tossed vertically (a vertical line segment, speeding up on the way down). From directly above: the balloon moves along a straight line toward the target with equally spaced positions at equal time intervals (constant horizontal velocity). From the side: the balloon follows a parabolic arc: rising with slowing upward motion, a peak, then falling with increasing downward motion, with evenly spaced horizontal spacing between positions.

answer.html: Behind: vertical up-and-down line. Above: straight line, evenly spaced dots. Side: parabola.

items.title: Figure 2 (Identify): vertical velocity of two marbles after falling for 2.5 s

question.html: One marble is dropped from rest off a ledge. A second marble rolls off the same ledge horizontally. Find the vertical velocity of each marble after 2.5 s in the air (ignore air resistance).

body.html: Both marbles start with 𝑣<sub>𝑦𝑖</sub>= 0, 𝑎<sub>𝑦</sub>= −9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>, 𝑡= 2.5 s. Find 𝑣<sub>𝑦</sub>.
Both marbles have the same vertical motion (free fall from rest), so 𝑣<sub>𝑦</sub>= 𝑣<sub>𝑦𝑖</sub>+ 𝑎<sub>𝑦</sub>𝑡.

answer.html: about 25 m/s downward (for both marbles)

check.html: Free fall adds about 9.8 m/s of speed each second, so 2.5 s gives roughly 2.5 times 9.8, which is about 25 m/s.

items.title: Get It? Explain why a paintball shot horizontally and a paintball dropped from the same height at the same instant hit the ground at the same time

body.html: A horizontal launch gives no initial vertical velocity, and the only force is gravity, which is vertical. The horizontal motion does not change the vertical forces.

answer.html: Both paintballs start with zero vertical velocity, feel the same downward acceleration, and fall the same height, so they take the same time to reach the ground. Only the horizontal distance differs.

items.title: Figure 3 (Decide): a dart is thrown upward on the Moon, where 𝑔Moon = 1.62 m/s2. What is the value of 𝑎𝑦 at the top of its path?

answer.html: 𝑎<sub>𝑦</sub>= −1.62 m/s<sup>2</sup> (1.62 m/s² downward, with up taken as positive). The acceleration is the same everywhere along the path, including the top, even though 𝑣<sub>𝑦</sub>= 0 there.

items.title: Get It? Explain why the horizontal motion of a golf ball in flight is constant

answer.html: After the club loses contact there is no horizontal force (air resistance is ignored; gravity is vertical), so by Newton's first and second laws the horizontal acceleration is zero and the horizontal velocity does not change.

items.title: Get It? Describe why, in a motion diagram of a thrown dart, the vertical velocity arrows change length but the horizontal velocity arrows do not

answer.html: Gravity pulls down, so the vertical velocity changes by 9.8 m/s every second (arrows shrink on the way up and grow on the way down). There is no horizontal force, so the horizontal arrows all stay the same length.

items.title: Crosscutting Concept: Patterns (launch a spring-loaded toy at various angles)

question.html: What is missing: This asks you to do a hands-on investigation (launch an object and record it), which cannot be done here. Expected result (representative, not measured): Every launch gives a parabola. At a fixed launch speed the range is largest at 45°, and angles that add to 90° (such as 20° and 70°) give equal ranges but different heights and flight times; the larger angle goes higher and stays up longer.

answer.html: All launches trace parabolas; complementary angles give equal ranges; 45° gives the maximum range.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1), Problem 7: two arrows are shot horizontally from the same height at a target 20 m away, one at 40 m/s and one at 65 m/s

question.html: Which arrow hits the target lower, and why?

body.html: Both arrows fall under the same gravity, so 𝛥𝑦=<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>𝑔𝑡<sup>2</sup>, but they spend different times in the air: 𝑡= 𝑑/ 𝑣<sub>𝑥</sub>.
The slower arrow takes longer to travel the distance 𝑑 to the target, so it has more time to fall: 𝛥𝑦=<sub> </sub><sup>𝑔𝑑</sup><sup>2</sup>
<sub>2</sub>, which is larger for smaller 𝑣<sub>𝑥</sub>. (Numerically: 𝑡= 0.50 s and a drop of 1.2 m for the 40 m/s arrow, and 𝑡= 0.31 s and a drop of 0.46 m for the 65 m/s arrow.)

answer.html: The 40 m/s arrow hits lower. It spends more time in the air before reaching the target, so gravity pulls it down farther; the faster arrow gets there sooner and falls less.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1), Problem 8: free-body and motion diagrams of an air- hockey puck sliding off the edge of a table

question.html: The puck slides at constant speed across a frictionless table and then leaves the edge. Draw free-body and motion diagrams for two points on the table and two points in the air.

Two points on the table: Free-body diagram: weight (down) and normal force (up) of equal length; no friction. Net force is zero. Motion diagram: equal-length velocity vectors pointing along the direction of motion, no acceleration vector. Two points in the air: Free-body diagram: only the weight, pointing down (the table's normal force is gone). Motion diagram: the horizontal velocity component is the same length at both points; the downward velocity component gets longer; the acceleration vector 𝑎 points down.

answer.html: On the table: 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>, net force zero, constant velocity. In the air: only 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub> downward, constant horizontal velocity, downward acceleration of 9.8 m/s².

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1), Problem 9: a stone is thrown from a 36.0-m high bridge at 10.0 m/s, 30.0° below the horizontal

question.html: How far from the base of the bridge, horizontally, does it land in the water?

Use vertical motion (a quadratic in 𝑡) to find the time, then use constant horizontal velocity.
(The negative root is rejected.)

answer.html: about 19.5 m

check.html: Dropping 36 m alone would take about 2.7 s; the downward throw shortens the time to 2.25 s, so a range of about 19.5 m is reasonable.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1), Problem 11 (Critical Thinking): the same throw on Mars, where 𝑔Mars = 3.71 m/s2

question.html: An astronaut throws a ball with the same speed and angle on Mars as on Earth (𝑔= 9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>). How do the initial velocity components, the time of flight, the maximum height, and the range compare with Earth?

body.html: Initial velocity components are unchanged. Only 𝑎<sup>𝑦</sup> changes, from 𝑔 to 𝑔<sub>Mars</sub>, so everything that depends on 1 / 𝑔 grows by the factor 𝑔/ 𝑔<sub>Mars</sub>.
The ratio is <sup>9.80</sup> <sup>3.71</sup> = 2.64. Time of flight 𝑡= 2𝑣<sup>𝑦𝑖</sup>/ 𝑔, maximum height 𝑦<sub>max</sub> = 𝑣<sup>𝑦𝑖</sup>

and range 𝑅= 𝑣<sub>𝑥</sub>𝑡= 2𝑣<sub>𝑥</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑦𝑖</sub>/ 𝑔 are each proportional to 1 / 𝑔, so each becomes 2.64 times larger. The horizontal velocity is unchanged, and the initial vertical velocity is the same, but it changes only 3.71 / 9.80 = 0.379 as fast.

answer.html: Initial vertical (and horizontal) velocity: same. Vertical velocity at a later time: decreases only about 0.38 times as fast. Time of flight: 2.64 times longer. Maximum height: 2.64 times higher. Horizontal distance (range): 2.64 times larger.

check.html: A throw that goes 20 m on Earth would go about 53 m on Mars, which fits the weaker gravity.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1), Problem 7: baseballs pitched horizontally at different speeds

body.html: Both balls fall under the same gravity from the same height, so for equal times they fall equal distances: 𝛥𝑦=<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>𝑔𝑡<sup>2</sup>. They have different times of flight to reach the plate, though: 𝑡= 𝑑/ 𝑣<sub>𝑥</sub>.

The slower ball takes longer to travel the distance 𝑑 to the plate, so it has more time to fall: 𝛥𝑦=<sub> </sub><sup>𝑔𝑑</sup><sup>2</sup> <sup>2</sup><sup>𝑣</sup><sub>𝑥</sub> <sub>2</sub>, which is larger for smaller 𝑣<sub>𝑥</sub>.

answer.html: The slower ball spends more time in the air before reaching the plate, so gravity pulls it down farther; the faster ball gets there sooner and falls less.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1), Problem 8: free-body and motion diagrams of the sliding ice cube

question.html: Two points on the table: Free-body diagram: weight (down) and normal force (up) of equal length; no friction. Net force is zero. Motion diagram: equal-length velocity vectors pointing along the direction of motion, no acceleration vector. Two points in the air: Free-body diagram: only the weight, pointing down (the table's normal force is gone). Motion diagram: the horizontal velocity component is the same length at both points; the downward velocity component gets longer; acceleration vector 𝑎 points down.

answer.html: On the table: 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>, net force zero, constant velocity. In the air: only 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub> downward, constant horizontal velocity, downward acceleration of 9.8 m/s².

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1), Problem 9: ball thrown from a 28-m window at

question.html: 15.0 m/s, 20.0° below horizontal

body.html: 𝑣<sup>𝑖</sup>= 15.0 m/s, 𝜃= −20.0°, 𝑦<sub>𝑖</sub>= 0, 𝑦<sub>𝑓</sub>= −28 m, 𝑎<sub>𝑦</sub>= −9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>. Find horizontal distance 𝑥.
Use vertical motion (a quadratic in 𝑡) to find the time, then use constant horizontal velocity.
(The negative root is rejected.)

answer.html: about 27 m

check.html: Dropping 28 m alone would take about 2.4 s; the downward throw shortens the time to 1.9 s, so a range of about 27 m is reasonable.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1), Problem 10: maximum height of a softball thrown at

question.html: 11.0 m/s, 50.0° above horizontal

body.html: 𝑣<sup>𝑖</sup>= 11.0 m/s, 𝜃= 50.0°, 𝑣<sup>𝑦</sup>= 0 at the top. Find 𝑦<sub>max</sub> above the launch point.
Only the vertical component matters: 0 = 𝑣<sub>𝑦𝑖</sub>

answer.html: 3.62 m (above the release point)

check.html: A ball thrown at about 11 m/s rises a few meters, which is typical.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1), Problem 11 (Critical Thinking): same throw on the Moon, where 𝑔Moon = 𝑔/ 6

body.html: Initial velocity components are unchanged. Only 𝑎<sub>𝑦</sub> changes, from 𝑔 to 𝑔/ 6, so everything that depends on 1 / 𝑔 grows by 6.

Time of flight 𝑡= 2𝑣<sup>𝑦𝑖</sup>/ 𝑔, maximum height 𝑦<sub>max</sub> = 𝑣<sup>𝑦𝑖</sup> <sup>2</sup> / 2𝑔, range 𝑅= 𝑣<sub>𝑥</sub>𝑡= 2𝑣<sub>𝑥</sub>𝑣<sub>𝑦𝑖</sub>/ 𝑔. Each is proportional to 1 / 𝑔, so each becomes 6 times larger. The horizontal velocity is unchanged, and the initial vertical velocity is the same, but it changes 6 times more slowly (so the vertical velocity at a given time is larger in magnitude on the Moon).

answer.html: Initial vertical (and horizontal) velocity: same. Vertical velocity at a later time: decreases only one-sixth as fast. Time of flight: 6 times longer. Maximum height: 6 times higher. Horizontal distance (range): 6 times larger.

check.html: A hit that travels 64 m on Earth would travel about 390 m on the Moon, which matches the well- known long Moon golf shots.
